script.title: Understanding Stacks and Their Operations
segments: Today, we'll be reviewing the key concepts of stacks and their operations, including array-based and linked stacks, as well as their uses in various applications.
A stack is a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure, meaning that the last element added is the first one to be removed, similar to a pile of plates.
The stack operations include push, pop, and peek, all of which have a time complexity of O(1), making them efficient for handling large amounts of data.
An array-based stack uses an array and a top index to store and retrieve elements, with push operations writing elements at the top and incrementing the top index.

Alternatively, a linked stack uses nodes to store elements, with each push operation creating a new node pointing to the previous top element, allowing for dynamic memory allocation and no fixed capacity.

Stacks have numerous applications, including maintaining undo history, implementing the call stack in programming languages, checking balanced brackets in parsing, and performing Depth-First Search (DFS) in graph traversal.
For example, when checking balanced brackets, we can push every opening bracket onto the stack and then pop and compare with the corresponding closing bracket.
Recap: A stack is a LIFO data structure with O(1) time complexity operations, and it has various applications in programming, including undo history, call stack, and balanced brackets checking.
